title: Shopping Offers Problem

notes: A special offer can be used only when every item quantity in the offer fits within the remaining needs.
The goal is to buy exactly the requested quantities at minimum cost.
The same special offer may be used multiple times.

content.problemStatement:
In LeetCode Store, there are n items to sell. Each item has a price. However, there are some special offers, and a special offer consists of one or more different kinds of items with a sale price.

You receive an integer array price where price[i] is the price of the ith item, and an integer array needs where needs[i] is the number of pieces of the ith item you want to buy.

You are also given an array special where special[i] is of size n + 1 where special[i][j] is the number of pieces of the jth item in the ith offer and special[i][n] (i.e., the last integer in the array) is the price of the ith offer.

Output the lowest price you have to pay for exactly certain items as given, where you could make optimal use of the special offers. You are not allowed to buy more items than you want, even if that would lower the overall price. You could use any of the special offers as many times as you want.

 

Example 1:

Input: price = [2,5], special = [[3,0,5],[1,2,10]], needs = [3,2]
Output: 14
Explanation: There are two kinds of items, A and B. Their prices are $2 and $5 respectively. 
In special offer 1, you can pay $5 for 3A and 0B
In special offer 2, you can pay $10 for 1A and 2B. 
You need to buy 3A and 2B, so you may pay $10 for 1A and 2B (special offer #2), and $4 for 2A.

Example 2:

Input: price = [2,3,4], special = [[1,1,0,4],[2,2,1,9]], needs = [1,2,1]
Output: 11
Explanation: The price of A is $2, and $3 for B, $4 for C. 
You may pay $4 for 1A and 1B, and $9 for 2A ,2B and 1C. 
You need to buy 1A ,2B and 1C, so you may pay $4 for 1A and 1B (special offer #1), and $3 for 1B, $4 for 1C. 
You cannot add more items, though only $9 for 2A ,2B and 1C.

 

Constraints:

  • n == price.length == needs.length
  • 1 <= n <= 6
  • 0 <= price[i], needs[i] <= 10
  • 1 <= special.length <= 100
  • special[i].length == n + 1
  • 0 <= special[i][j] <= 50
  • The input is generated that at least one of special[i][j] is non-zero for 0 <= j <= n - 1.

notes: Offers that are more expensive than buying the same quantities individually can simply be skipped by the minimum calculation.
Memoization is the key optimization because many sequences of offers reach the same remaining-needs state.
solution.approach: Use depth-first search with memoization over the remaining needs. For each state, first consider buying all remaining items individually. Then try every special offer that does not exceed the remaining needs, recursively solve the reduced needs, and take the minimum total cost. Memoizing each needs state prevents recomputing the same subproblem.

better.complexity: Still exponential in the worst case, but substantially fewer branches are explored because invalid offers are discarded immediately.
better.description: Use DFS and prune any special offer that would make a remaining need negative. This avoids invalid branches but can still recompute the same remaining-needs state many times.

optimal.complexity: O(S * N * P) time and O(N * P) space in the memo-state upper bound, where P = product(needs[i] + 1).
optimal.description: Represent each subproblem by the remaining needs vector and memoize its minimum cost. The base cost for a state is the sum of price[i] * needs[i]. For every usable special offer, subtract its item counts and combine its price with the memoized cost of the new state. The minimum over these choices is optimal.

bruteForce.complexity: Exponential in the number of reachable offer-use states.
bruteForce.description: Enumerate every possible sequence of special-offer uses and finish the remaining needs with individual purchases. Without memoization, identical remaining-needs states may be solved repeatedly.

solution.timeComplexity: O(S * N * P) in a coarse upper bound over P = product(needs[i] + 1) memo states, where S is the number of special offers and N is the number of item types.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(P * N) for memoized needs states and recursion depth up to O(N * max(needs)) in the worst case; with the standard tuple-state memoization, the dominant storage is the memo table.

followUps: How would you change the solution if the quantities in needs could be much larger than 10?
What pruning rule can remove offers that are never cheaper than individual purchases?
Could the same memoized state technique be implemented iteratively?
